member of the commission. madam president, first of all i would like to say to mr le hyaric, who is asking for surplus food to be sent to haiti, that this is not the approach of the european union, for the simple reason that the commission prefers to buy these products in the region. we'll see if we can get them locally first instead of having to ship our surplus to haiti. secondly, regarding the whole matter of coordination and civil protection and so on, let me just say three things. firstly, civil protection is a competence of the member states, and all coordination initiatives must be built on this basis. this was also proposed by the barnier report but up to now we have not reached a conclusion. it is a matter for the member states and not for the commission as such. secondly, as far as civil protection and its coordination is concerned, since the 2004 tsunami eu civil protection coordination has grown stronger and much more efficient. virtual exercises can of course never test enough the effectiveness of our cooperation as much as natural disasters do, sadly enough. in this crisis non-eu member states are calling the mic to see how they can contribute to the relief effort with eu facilities. thirdly, let us not forget that in the second barroso commission humanitarian aid and civil protection have been combined under one commissioner, which i think is a very valuable effort. in addition we also now have a high representative, who will have a double hat. what we have seen in the past about coordination is that it is not lacking within the commission for example - i will come back to that in a minute - but it is sometimes between the european institutions and the member states and between the european commission and council. the whole idea behind this double-hatting was precisely that the council and commission could work better together, and i think it has been demonstrated in this crisis that this has, in fact, been quite an advance. lastly, i would also like to say that i am a little bit sad about what some speakers have said. of course as a commissioner i cannot be sad, i just have to take notice of it, but it does not pay enough tribute to all our people who have been working, on the spot and in brussels, from hour one, day and night, during the weekend, without any complaint, without asking for any compensation. they have been working very hard and within hours they were also active on the spot, although their facilities were also hit hard. so please consider that this is the kind of massive disaster that is not predictable, that you can only respond to when it happens, and for which you have to demonstrate that you can organize a response in a very short period of time. i think the commission has been demonstrating this. i think that the member states immediately and massively supported our action and i think we should also be a little bit less critical about those services.

acting president of the council. - the treaties of the european union provide for a clear division of powers. the economic policies of the member states are of common interest to the union, but at the same time national budgets are the responsibility of the member states. since there is a single currency in 16 countries of the union and at the same time a plan to extend it, since the idea of monetary union is something that appears in the maastricht treaty as an objective as all-encompassing as possible, there is naturally a respect for the rules of the states in relation to their budgets, because that affects the whole of the european economy and monetary system. excessive government deficits must therefore be avoided, which is essential for the functioning of economic and monetary union, in which monetary union has developed - and this must be acknowledged - above all, not economic union. the stability pact is the reason why, in maastricht at the time, now in the treaty on the functioning of the european union, article 123 prohibits overdrafts or the granting of credit for such overdrafts by the european central bank and the central banks of the member states whose currency is the euro. the treaty also states that neither the union nor the member states shall assume or be liable for the commitments of central governments or other public authorities of another member state. so each member state has to guarantee its debt obligations and the council has said that all member states must do so and the council continues to trust that greece and the other member states will take the appropriate decisions to correct the economic imbalances, to preserve the soundness of the national economic and financial environment. it should be recalled that the excessive deficit procedure provides for economic policy monitoring in justified cases. the council will discuss the greek case 'hopefully' in february. it is likely that at that time, pending the commission's right of initiative, recommendations will be adopted and strategies will therefore be devised, a way in which the european union can express its interest, its involvement in the difficult situations or circumstances that some of its member states may be experiencing.

cohesion in the union. all this is what we can call economic union, the internal economic cohesion of the union. that is where we must go, with clear political leadership from the union, which is already taking place. we must reflect on the fact that the day after tomorrow the spanish presidency of the union will meet - and that is the first thing to do - the informal european council will growth pact, but also extending it. i agree with those of you who have said that it is not just a question of pursuing a fiscal and budgetary policy in accordance with our rules, but that we must go the new greek government corrected the notification we had received a few days before the elections, changing the deficit from 6% to 12.7% in three weeks! and it wasn't just about statistical corrections. in that huge slide in the deficit in greece, there has been a great deal of a complete lack of control over budgetary policy. that's not a statistical subject. do not ask eurostat to solve it. that's a management issue, a government issue, that let revenue fall or did nothing when revenue fell and let spending rise or pushed spending up because the election was coming. i want to make it clear that this is what happened. moreover, in relation to statistical problems, and in reply to mr martin - as mr karas has reminded me - at the end of 2004, i, on behalf of the commission, proposed to the council that eurostat be given greater scope for carrying out audits in cases where there are statistical problems which cannot be solved by means of normal notifications. eurostat does not compile the data. eurostat receives notifications from the member states. to see beyond the notifying authority, eurostat needs powers which it does not have and the commission asked for those powers and the council did not give them. and i have told the council that we are going to ask for those powers again: my colleague olli rehn, who will be responsible for economic and monetary affairs from tomorrow without any further transitions, has the proposal ready for the new commission to adopt at its first formal meeting, once you have been so kind as to approve it today. after that acting president of the council. - madam president, ladies and gentlemen, it is a great honour for me to be here on behalf of the presidency of the council. i very much appreciate your interest in the positions to be taken at the next conference of the parties to the cites convention, the convention on international trade in endangered species of wild fauna and flora, to be held in doha, qatar, from 13 to 25 march. the council considers the washington convention to be a fundamental instrument for the protection of endangered species of flora and fauna, and therefore it is incumbent upon us to play an active role in ensuring that cites remains an effective tool for its dual purpose of conservation and sustainable management of natural resources. in this respect, it should be remembered that the european union applies more restrictive rules than the convention itself, using the precautionary principle to maintain or, where appropriate, reduce the loss of biodiversity. the next conference of the parties to the convention, to be held in doha in march, the so-called cop xv, provides a great opportunity for us to discuss a number of proposals to modify the classification of different species of flora and fauna in the appendices of the convention according to their degree of threat, as well as other proposals to improve the implementation and observance of the convention. member of the commission. − madam president, the forthcoming 15th conference of parties indeed offers a unique window of opportunity to improve the conservation and status of a wide number of species affected by trade. the european union is one of the major markets for wildlife products. therefore it has a specific responsibility to ensure that wildlife trade is sustainable and that robust international rules are adopted within the cites convention to that effect. it is a priority for the commission to make sure that international trade is not detrimental to the survival of endangered plants and animal species. in this respect the eu has been playing a leading role within cites and will continue to do so at the next meeting. the commission will in the coming days adopt a proposal for the eu position in view of this meeting. the common eu position will then be adopted by the council. in its discussions with the member states, the commission will make sure that the final common position supports ambitious and science-based measures. i would also like to thank parliament for its position on the most salient issues which will be discussed at the cites conference of parties. this resolution sends a clear message which we will need to take into consideration. while the detailed position of the european union has not been finalised yet, i can explain the principles and priorities which will guide our decisions on the most sensitive issues to be discussed in doha. in the first place, the european union considers that cites is an appropriate instrument to regulate trade in all species which are affected by trade. this is the case for terrestrial as well as for marine species and for species subject to important commercial interests or not. in that vein the european union has tabled proposals to regulate trade in two shark species: porbeagle and spiny dogfish. it is of the utmost importance that sharks at last receive the protection they deserve after decades of overfishing. a listing under cites appendix ii would put an end to unregulated international trade in shark products which is one of the key drivers of their exploitation. with such listing, trade in those shark products will only take place if they stem from sustainable managed stocks. the european union is also proposing to arrange for the protection afforded by cites to the tiger, which is one of the most endangered species in the world. 2010 is the international year for tigers and is a perfect opportunity to strengthen the current mechanisms in cites to allow for a merciless fight against illegal trade in this species and improved transparency in range states on how the tiger populations are conserved. i would also like to touch upon some of the other important proposals which parliament has also clearly identified. the first is atlantic bluefin tuna. i have to repeat here that there is no final position on this issue. what i can tell you is that there is concern within the commission on the current state of the stock and that we are working hard to find an appropriate proposal that will help properly address this problem at the international level. the final commission position will take account of the latest scientific information on the stock and of the outcome of the meeting of the international commission for the conservation of atlantic tuna which took place in november last year. the second is elephants and the ivory trade. this has been a longstanding, contentious issue within cites, especially among african countries themselves. the commission is very worried about the high level of poaching for elephants and illegal ivory trade which has been observed recently. the protection afforded to elephants needs to be reinforced, and the commission will not support solutions which would present a risk of increasing poaching. in that context we believe that it would not be appropriate that the next conference of parties agrees on a resumption of the commercial ivory trade. we also consider that proposals submitted to cites with a view to downlisting some elephant populations from cites appendix i to appendix ii need to be assessed objectively on the basis of the rules agreed within cites. allow me now to say a few words about the proposal by the usa related to the prohibition of international trade in polar bears. we are all aware that the ice melting in the arctic is a dramatic threat for the survival of this species. this needs to be addressed first and foremost via a very ambitious policy on climate change and i think that the eu has clearly shown the way to go in the matter. we also believe that it is worth checking how any additional threat to this species might be mitigated. international trade is limited but might exacerbate the pressure on the species. our final position will depend on how the measure proposed by the united states provides real benefits for the conservation of a species. finally, on the question of corals, there is no doubt that red and pink corals have been overharvested in many regions of the world. at the last cites meeting in 2007, the european union backed a proposal by the united states to regulate international trade in both species and we have again co-sponsored a usa proposal for cop15. i believe that the european union should be consistent in this support as the new information available does not show improvement in the situation. i would also like to stress that such regulation would by no means result in the prohibition of trade but would just make sure that trade is possible when it is sustainable.
the s&d group is calling for a new approach to the problem of the environment. mr president, mr leinen has covered the rest, so i shall concentrate mainly on the tuna issue. let's really look at it from a scientific point of view. the bluefin tuna is in immediate danger of extinction. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's trade policy is not distorted by the introduction of a new trade policy. the scientific secretariat of cites, in a communication last week, is proposing to include tuna in appendix i, which means banning international trade. it says in particular that: 'the secretariat concurs with the majority of fao ad hoc expert advisory panel that these species meet the criteria for inclosing appendix i. the proposal is based on the fao proposal, which is based on the iccat proposal. the scientific part of the debate is therefore closed. let us look at it from a political and social point of view. the tuna stocks are collapsing. scientific bodies argue that if international trade is not banned, there will be no bluefin tuna in a few years. the fisheries regulation has so far failed to deliver. instead of the 19000 tonnes of bluefin tuna proposed by iccat for 2008, it is estimated that 50,000 tonnes were caught. we propose to stop international trade today, while we have time to save the tuna; the commission has already taken the necessary steps to ensure that the european union can continue to trade within the european union, which is not affected by cites, and at the same time to compensate the fishermen and businesses affected by the export ban. the s & d group has tabled an amendment to this effect. this will restore the stocks of bluefin tuna and allow trade to resume. to this end, it is exceptionally provided that the ban on international trade may be lifted immediately once tuna catches have been restored, instead of gradually for the other species. if international trade is not banned, then bluefin tuna stocks will collapse, the fishing industry will be destroyed forever and then no one will be entitled to compensation. the commission has already taken a number of measures to protect the fishermen of the mediterranean, and i am sure that the commission will be able to support the amendments tabled by the committee on fisheries. otherwise, jobs will be lost forever and a beautiful and unique way of life will be lost.
mr president, colleagues have already tackled the issue from all angles. i would like to say that i support the positions that mr milana has just expressed, and we must bear in mind that the inclusion of bluefin tuna in annex i will have many socioeconomic consequences, such as the bankruptcy and closure of many enterprises, especially small and mediumsized ones, the loss of jobs and a reduction in europe's competitiveness. we must remember that bluefin tuna supplies a market worth 6 billion euros worldwide. i would really like to hear some scientifically based proposals to ensure the future sustainability of bluefin tuna populations, but which also take into account the sustainability of european fishermen and their families. in my view, the best and most adequate way is to include it in annex ii. the european union is not fishing alone, either in the mediterranean or in the atlantic. the bluefin tuna fishery is a global activity. european fishermen face strong, often unfair, competition from north african countries. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the fisheries sector is not left behind. we have to make sure that everyone plays the game by the same rules. it may also be of some interest that japan has 30,000 tons of bluefin tuna frozen and the ban may lead to the stockpiles costing from $10 billion to $20 billion today.

acting president of the council. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to begin this debate by thanking parliament for the possibility of a calm debate on counter-terrorism policy and on some of the elements of that policy in particular, and to do so when a reasonable amount of time has passed since the shock that the failed attack in detroit last december caused throughout the world. i am, of course, in favour of reacting when something like this happens, but i am much more in favour of working continuously, calmly - 'no hurry but no rest', as we say in my country - when it comes to dealing with a threat such as the terrorist threat, which, i must say in this house, has not diminished in any of the countries of the european union. we know that terrorists are watching us, we know that they are innovating, that they are trying to change their ways of acting to circumvent our counterterrorism strategies. this strategy must therefore also innovate and change, it must also improve and, above all, it must learn from the mistakes, some of which we make. that said, it is clear that if there had not been a failed bombing in detroit in december, we would probably not be at this moment debating the terms on which we are going to do it in this house. i am not saying that the commission should not be involved in the debate on the future of the community, but that it should be involved in the debate on the future of the community. the debate we are having here today is based on an analysis of what went wrong in that alleged attack and what measures the various countries are taking to prevent such mistakes from being repeated. and that's why we talk about data analysis, and that's why we talk about counterterrorism services and the common analysis of the data that each of them has, and that's why we also talk about body scanners. we're talking about flaws detected in an attack that, fortunately, never happened. if this is the debate, then i will begin by stating to the house the most obvious conclusions which i believe we can draw from the failed bombing in detroit. that's five. first, detroit shows that civil aviation remains a top target for terrorists. second, detroit shows that collecting data is important, but integrating and analyzing it is even more important. thirdly, detroit demonstrates that al qaeda affiliates are willing to strike outside what we might call their own territory. this is the case with al qaeda in the arabian peninsula (the alleged terrorist organisation behind the failed bombing in detroit) or al qaeda in the islamic maghreb, which poses a threat to all. fourthly, detroit reminds us of the importance of working on the processes of radicalization. the personality of the alleged terrorist i think is very striking in relation to this issue. and finally, detroit calls for us to look carefully, attentively, at failed states or those states which, because of their circumstances, might become so. the first and second conclusions - the danger that continues to threaten civil aviation and the need to integrate the information we have - lead directly to this evening's debate, or to the two debates this afternoon: on information and its use and on body scanners. i must say that this is not a new debate, nor is it the first time that it has been debated in this house. for example, in the debate on the last report by the coordinator for the fight against terrorism, mr de kerchove, here in this house on 26 november - a report which is certainly interesting and clear - there was talk of information management and there was also talk of the protection of personal data, because, in fact, information and the analysis of that information are, as we have had occasion to discuss here this afternoon, fundamental parts of the fight to prevent and prosecute terrorism. we must identify the terrorists; we must know where they may be carrying out the attack, who or who is supplying them with weapons; we must know the material infrastructure on which they rely; we must know their communication systems; and all this through databases and specialised sources. to have all this information available, we have to exchange it among ourselves and we have to manage that exchange of information properly. it is true - and i hasten to say it - that some of the attacks we have suffered in the past could have been avoided if the information had been made available to those with counter-terrorism responsibility in a timely manner, in other words, if the information had been able to be handled comprehensively, intelligently - if i may use the expression - which is not always the case. and that brings us to the debate of information management. to exchange information and to do so properly, we have within the framework of the european union a strategy which we have recently adopted - in fact it is part of the council conclusions of last november - which precisely tries to make available to the security forces and the intelligence services the data necessary for the sake of usefulness and effectiveness in the fight against terrorism: the necessary data and only those, no more, because the abundance of data sometimes goes in the opposite direction to the effectiveness in using them. as stated in that strategy, the aim is that decisions on the exchange of information are taken in a consistent, professional, efficient, cost-effective, reliable and understandable way for all citizens and all professionals using it. a strategy, it says, which must take account - as is also reflected in many of the statements of this house - of the needs of the fight against terrorism, as well as, or at the same time, the rights of individuals, the right to privacy, the right to the protection of their personal data, which we have dealt with this afternoon. as i said at the beginning, another lesson we can draw from the alleged bombing in detroit is that commercial aircraft are still a prime target of terrorists and it is clear that the alleged terrorist managed to get on the plane with enough explosives to blow it up in the air by bypassing all our surveillance systems, all the systems or security devices at our airports. in other words, it is clear that we must proceed to review these security arrangements because they have clearly been insufficient to prevent an attack which, fortunately, did not take place, such as the alleged attack in detroit. in short, we must continue to improve our security services to try to prevent terrorists or suspected terrorists from boarding commercial aircraft. we must do so to prevent anyone from being able to board an aircraft with weapons, with explosives or with precursors of those explosives. and if we can't do either, we have to protect our planes so they can't suffer mishaps in flight. and this is precisely the framework of the debate in which the issue of body scanners, which is of concern to this house and also to the council, is being discussed. as you know, the commission has the power to set objectives and to lay down rules on this matter of aviation safety. these matters are discussed in the informal and formal transport ministers' council. however, i must tell you that this subject, that of air safety, was discussed at the informal council of ministers held a few weeks ago in toledo. and we have agreed on several things in this council: firstly, that it is desirable and necessary to have a common position within the european union on these body scanners and, in general, on all the security mechanisms at our airports; that it is pointless for some airports to be less protected than others because this simply makes us all, in the end, less protected. we would therefore like this to be a debate in which there is agreement, a common position of the european union. secondly, it is a difficult and delicate subject, and there are various aspects to be considered: first, of course, to know how effective this type of scanner is in preventing terrorists with explosives or with explosives precursors from boarding aircraft. the second is to know and analyse in depth the compatibility of these scanners with the right to privacy and the privacy of individuals, which is of concern to the council, the commission and this house. and the third is to know the relationship that might exist between the use of these scanners and the health of those who go through them to board commercial airplanes. on these three issues - the effectiveness of body scanners in particular, their impact on health and whether or not they are compatible with the fundamental rights and freedoms of citizens - the commission is working on three studies which it will make available to the council and this house shortly. for this reason, the informal council in toledo agreed to wait until these elements were available to hold an in-depth debate which would enable us to reach, achieve, reach a unanimous position on this matter, which would be very desirable. in this position, we will take very much into account the resolution that this parliament adopted on 23 october 2008 in a debate on body scanners, which dealt precisely with the impact assessment on rights, the necessary consultations with the european data protection supervisor, the health implications and the economic impact. these are also considerations which must be taken into account in our future debate. i would like to thank the house again for the opportunity to discuss these matters and the president for his flexibility over time.
member of the commission. − mr president, we are here to present a combined view on certain aspects in the fight against terrorism. my priority as transport commissioner is definitely the safety and security of passengers. this is a major priority for our common transport policy and this is always extremely important. the attempted terrorist attack on northwest airlines flight 253 to detroit on 25 december has again confirmed the reality of the threat to civil aviation. i would like to stress that existing eu standards on aviation security were correctly implemented on 25 december at amsterdam schiphol airport. the incident showed first of all the failure of intelligence, a failure ‘to connect the dots’. aviation remains a target for terrorists. we cannot ignore this fact. aviation security must therefore be guaranteed by all appropriate means, in full compliance with fundamental rights. the travelling public, the media and aviation stakeholders all legitimately ask us whether the existing security arrangements are good enough, or whether we need to take further action. in this regard, the new screening technologies, the so-called ‘body scanners’, are discussed everywhere today. regarding the use of body scanners at airports, aviation security experts are of the opinion that these machines have better detection capacity than current screening equipment. some think that they are considerably better. some think that this is not such a big advance, but how big the added value of these machines is to airport security and what the consequences are for health and privacy is not yet entirely clear today. as noted previously by parliament in 2008, the use of body-imaging technology raises a number of questions, notably in relation to privacy, data protection and health. i intend to present to you in april a report on imaging technology and its use at eu airports. this report will address the questions raised in the european parliament resolution of 2008. we need to look at these questions seriously. we also need to make up our minds on whether these concerns are better addressed at national or european level. to my mind, an eu framework would be better. i say this based on our experience of a common approach since 9/11 and with a view to the efficiency of the single market for aviation. an eu framework guarantees uniform standards in relation both to security and to respect for individual rights. finally, i would like to underline that airport security is a much larger question than the introduction of a new screening technology. to fight terrorism targeting civil aviation, we need a large variety of combined and coordinated measures – intelligence, profiling, different search methods and international cooperation. as the minister just said, terrorists develop. we must develop as well, and body scanners are only one element in this variety. i look forward to your views and thank you for your attention.
member of the commission. − mr president, this is the commission’s new dual approach. as the former debate showed, now that we have the lisbon treaty, work at eu level now enters into a new phase. i am very happy and honoured that i will work together with you in the fight against terrorism and on other security-related matters. we will do this while of course fully respecting that it is the member states who have the final responsibility for all operational and intelligence work in this field. i would like to recall to you – some of you were at my hearing a few weeks ago – that i made a promise that i would do an evaluation of all counter-terrorism policies. as a first step, i have asked my services to prepare an overview and an assessment of everything that has been achieved so far. this will be the basis upon which i will decide how to move forward. we need to evaluate and to get a full understanding of what we have, its effects, what is possibly missing and what is overlapping in order to be able to propose new measures and more thought through measures. i look forward to bringing this evaluation to you and to discussing it with you. but this stocktaking does not mean that i am not fully aware of the fact that the threat of terrorism has not diminished. as my colleague, mr kallas, and the council presidency have said, we know that terrorism is still one of the greatest threats to our values and to our democracies. the denver flight showed that recently. we have statistics from europol showing that in 2008 eu member states reported a total of 515 failed or successfully perpetrated terrorist attacks within europe; 359 individuals were tried on terrorist charges in a total of 187 proceedings; 50% of these were related to al-qa’ida or islamist terrorism, and 39% to separatist terrorism, such as eta activities in spain. we also know that in 2008 we had the tragic events and the horrible bombing in mumbai, which also targeted european citizens, among them members of this house. these events and the figures from europol speak a clear language: terrorism is still there, and it is important that we do not lower our guard and we ensure that all tools are deployed in the fight against terrorism, while of course always fully respecting fundamental rights. if we look at the instruments that we do have today we have the eu counter-terrorism strategy, developed after the attacks in madrid and in london. this strategy highlights the eu’s commitment to combating terrorism globally while respecting human rights and to making europe safer, allowing its citizens to live in an area of freedom, security and justice. this, of course, is a commitment that it still valid. there can be no freedom without security and there can be no security without freedom. that is why respecting fundamental rights in the fight against terrorism is not only a requirement of any democratic society but is a necessity in order to ensure that our policies remain credible, legitimate and sustainable. that is why the commission will only propose measures that will continue to be subject to eu law screening, especially with regard to fundamental rights and rigorous impact assessment, including the impact on personal data and individuals. terrorism is, as we know, a global phenomenon, and that is why we will remain dedicated to cooperating with our allies and partners and international organisations all over the world. regarding the internal dimension of countering and preventing terrorism, we do have in our counter-terrorist strategy some key objectives on how the union can contribute in the fight against terrorism. i fully share these objectives, in particular the need to stop violent radicalisation, protect our critical infrastructure, support victims, improve exchange of information between national authorities and cooperate with all appropriate stakeholders. we have to react to non-conventional threats and to improve the detection of threats. we have to deprive terrorists of financial resources and to invest more in research and technological development. this development on these policies has of course been strongly supported by the european commission in cooperation with the member states. over the past year, the commission has made a major contribution to approximating the legal frameworks of member states in this work. we have, for instance, the european arrest warrant, which created an eu-wide common understanding on terrorist crime and facilitated extradition procedures within the eu member states. we have also undertaken important activities to counter the terrorist abuse of the internet, addressing conditions conducive to terrorist radicalisation, launching a european programme for the protection of critical infrastructure, and limiting access by terrorists to the means they need to commit their acts – funding and explosives. the eu action plan for enhancing the security of explosives foresees important measures to raise the threshold for terrorists who want to use explosives for an attack. i would propose a legislative framework to address the dangers associated with precursors which can be used to fabricate improvised explosive devices. i will do so this year. we also have the cbrn action plan proposed by the commission last june and agreed by the council. this action plan consists of 130 measures. the commission has earmarked up to eur 100 million which could be made available from its existing financial programmes to facilitate implementation. i am fully committed to ensuring that, in the coming years, the european commission will continue to develop its role as facilitator and catalyst for cooperation, expert networks, exchanging best practices, pooling resources, improving research and developing common approaches to transnational challenges. we will also have to revise how we use our financial resources. this might be by creating an internal security fund, which is foreseen in the stockholm programme. on a large scale, international information exchange concerning the collection of data and storage of data concerning thousands of citizens has to take account – and this was very visible in the last debate we had – of very high data-protection standards in order to prevent abuse and mishandling. we also have to make sure, as commissioner kallas said, that we connect the dots in an appropriate way. together with my colleague, viviane reding, i will submit in the near future a combined data protection regime that would also cover police and judicial cooperation. all this will be considered in the evaluation and it will be under the umbrella of the internal security strategy that we will put forward to you within a short time. finally, let me conclude by underlining that, in the long run, we can only succeed in fighting against terrorism if we remain able to communicate our values and remain respectful of fundamental rights. we have to avoid our policies being perceived as ambiguous or as applying double standards. we can only defend high moral ground and prevent alienation from our societies and our way of living if we remain faithful to our values of democracy and the rule of law.
you gave us a very hopeful prospect. maybe one day we will have you, mr kallas and ms reding representing the commission at the same time.

acting president of the council. - mr president, i have listened carefully to the speeches of all the groups and all the members on this subject. i think it's been a tremendously interesting set of exhibitions, which i appreciate. i would like to stress, as i did in my first speech, that i am not in the least in favour of debates on such a complex and sensitive subject as the fight against terrorism following the attacks or the alleged attacks. it is clear that we have to examine these attacks or these alleged attacks to find out what went wrong with our security systems, but it is no less so because, as has been repeatedly pointed out here this afternoon, counter-terrorism policy must be a deliberate, calm, well-considered policy, applied proportionately. if we adopt measures which end up undermining our principles, we are probably making a big mistake. we must therefore analyse, for example, what happened in detroit, in order to try to avoid mistakes, but we must not act compulsively behind every attack, because this would probably lead us to take measures which, in some cases, simply would not make sense. europe has a strategy on counter-terrorism policy. we have a good strategy for combating terrorism in the european union. the strategy has proved effective in recent years: we need only look at the different actions of the security forces in the various countries and see to what extent these actions are often the result of the implementation of the common strategy we have had for some years now. we have a figure, a counterterrorism policy coordinator, whose speeches are interesting speeches. i would once again recommend that you study the last speech you made in this house in depth, because i think it is an excellent speech which shows concentrated much more on persecution. it is true that the most important thing in the face of terrorism is to prevent it: it is to prevent attacks. and that is why we are concentrating our joint efforts - again - on prevention. and that is why we are concerned about issues such as radicalisation, which i have mentioned in my speech and the commissioner has also mentioned. we are concerned to analyse the whole range of policies that we are implementing in each of the countries to prevent these processes of radicalisation, which are certainly at the root of a good part of the terrorist attacks we have suffered in recent years. we are also concerned about the proper exchange of information. it has been pointed out here on several occasions: the important thing is not to transmit all the information you have, the important thing is to transmit the relevant information to the one who is going to receive it. that's the information that needs to be passed on. it's not about stuffing ourselves with information. it is precisely the mechanisms for managing this information that make this exchange particularly effective. and in recent times we are making a lot of improvements in the european union in this area as well. we have a strategy which, if implemented, will make it possible, for example, for our information exchange systems to work better. and when i say information exchanging information and doing so more and more effectively. and finally, it is true that the controversy over body scanners is on the table, and i think, as i said in the first speech and as the commissioner and the commissioner have also said, that this is a subject we have to deal with and ideally we should find a common european formulation. it is true that if we do not find it, each country will be able to set its own policies and, probably, even if we did find it, there could be countries which, within the framework of their own law, could set their own policies. but there is no doubt that a common position on this matter would help us enormously. and to take that position, and in accordance with what i said at the beginning of this speech, it is good to have a calm and balanced debate, made up of three elements which are being studied by the commission at the moment: firstly, the effectiveness of these scanners (whether or not they are effective; what are the limits of these scanners and whether or not they are useful for what we want them to be useful for); secondly, their compatibility or not with fundamental rights, individual freedoms; and thirdly, their compatibility or not with the health of those who are going to pass through them. i think those are the three issues we need to study. once we have the reports on the table, we will adopt a common position which i think is necessary. mr president, i thank you once again for the speeches which have been made in this house and which i consider to be extremely useful for the work of the council.

member of the commission. − mr president, honourable members of the european parliament, the session went a little bit over time and the president of the commission had to leave because of other obligations, but it is an honour for me to answer on behalf of president barroso and on behalf of the commission. i would like to start by thanking you all for a fascinating debate, for many interesting ideas and for the enthusiasm and support you are showing for the eu 2020 strategy. without your support the eu 2020 cannot and will not succeed. i can assure you that the commission will be very bold; the eu 2020 will put citizens, employment and reduction of poverty at its core and centre. i can also assure you that we have learned the lessons of the lisbon strategy and therefore we will focus on a lesser number of targets and we will definitely improve on governance. at the commission we are very much encouraged by the strong interest and what we hope will be strong support from the european parliament. we are also very much encouraged by the sense of urgency in the european council where it is very clear that the atmosphere today is very different from that of five years ago when we were discussing the parameters of the lisbon strategy. but we need to do more; we need to get local and regional support for this strategy and most importantly we need to get the people behind it. we must make sure that they will not see it as another administrative exercise but that they will see it as an approach on how to improve life in europe and in their countries and regions. i would like to ask you, honourable members, to help us with this task. let us not compete among the institutions, let us cooperate, let us focus on the priorities and let us deliver the concrete results. in the eu 2020 strategy we would like to introduce a three-interlocking-pillar system based on a smart, greener and inclusive economy and we would like to build upon these pillars flexible initiatives which would be aimed at the bottlenecks, at the problems which are slowing the european economy, which are blocking it from using its full potential. we would like to focus more on education and training, so that the labour force in europe will maintain the competitive edge which europe deserves. we will keep the eu 2020 strategy linked with the stability and growth pact, because a solid fiscal position is key to the economic stability. we talked much today about greece and i would like to assure you that there was consensus that the euro area member states would take determined and coordinated action if needed to safeguard financial stability in the euro area. the commission will closely work together with greece and monitor how it implements the recommendations. a mission led by the commission with the ecb and drawing on the imf for technical support is now in athens to assess the need for greece to take additional measures. let me be very clear; president of the european council. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i am glad that we have had this debate, i am glad that i accepted your invitation to come here at the very beginning of the strategy 2020 process, because we are only at the very beginning of the discussion. we have just had a discussion on 11 february, we will have a spring council at the end of march and we will finalise the 2020 strategy, or the strategy for jobs and economic growth, in june. so we have a whole period to exchange views and to decide definitively on the action. i am therefore pleased with the european ambition that i have found here this afternoon and i am pleased with the sense of urgency that i have found here this afternoon. there is one intervention which i have nothing but contempt for, but i will not speak on that. as regards economic strategy, i shall distinguish between three periods. the first is the period we are still living through today, the financial crisis and all its consequences. let me use a different language from the one i heard this afternoon throughout the debate. let me explain. i also want to use language that reflects the positive aspects of the european union, because, you know, there are also positive things that have happened recently. we have learned the lessons of the crisis of the 1930s. we are now one year after the great recession, and, in fact, we are now back in 2010, in most countries, to positive growth. this was not done during the 1930s. the crisis actually lasted until the end of the decade. why is it that we have this positive growth now? because we took action. we've taken steps to save financial institutions, not because we love them so much as such, but because without them, there is no economy. we have been conducting a smart monetary policy. we have injected cash into the economy, which we did not do 70 years ago. at least one zone has been created for 16 countries, despite all the problems of monetary stability. in the 1930s, we had competitive devaluations. we didn't get them today. we have pursued a risky fiscal policy, using budget deficits to stimulate the economy. we have not done what we did in the 1930s, which was to return to a balanced budget as quickly as possible. so we have safeguarded our internal market, which is not perfect. we must look into this further and mr monti will make us concrete proposals. but we have not fallen back into the protectionism of the 1930s. and so, we've learned some lessons from the great crisis that we just experienced. i'm going to take this one step further. it is thanks to the european union that the g20 was born, that we took the initiative to create this embryo of world governance. this is the first time that the major powers, new and old, have come together to fight the crisis, in an imperfect way, but we will continue on this momentum. and so, europe, the european union is not ... we cannot always put the european union on the defensive. there are also some very positive things that have happened. now, we have to get out of this strategy, what is now called the exit strategy. we must find a balance between abandoning the fiscal stimulus too quickly and returning in the medium term to a balanced budget, which is absolutely necessary to finance our pension system, to finance our social security system, to finance our health care system. so it is a difficult balance to strike, and the stability and growth pact provides the means to do so, because it does not require an immediate return to budgetary equilibrium. it is a question of gradually reaching the 3% level first and then, in the medium term, reaching budgetary equilibrium. i believe that we have pursued and are pursuing a wise policy. so, as far as the lisbon strategy is concerned, we know its shortcomings, but we must not forget that the financial and economic crisis has totally disrupted the implementation of the lisbon agenda. there were, of course, gaps; we won't list them here, they're well known. but i want to say this: some major reforms are needed, or important reforms, and these important reforms, at european and national level, will require budgetary choices. it is not by chance, and i have repeated it in the conclusions in the letter which you have read, that we want to link the budgetary debate, in fact within the legal framework of the stability pact, to economic reforms. because if we say that more research and development, for example, must be done, then this must be included in national budgets and in the financial perspectives of the european union. this requires certain budgetary choices. another consequence of the choices we are making for the lisbon strategy is that not all the objectives we propose are always soft objectives. it could be, you figure, hard targets. that's when the hard part comes. there is the demand for reforms on the one hand and the implementation of reforms on the other. i do not say that i have heard it here, but outside this house, at european level, there are calls for tough measures, for major reforms, for hard reforms, and when you go back to your own country, i see little result from all this. so we need a consistent position. it is not only the european union that will be implementing reforms. we can encourage, encourage and supervise them, but it is at the national level that many reforms will have to be made and, therefore, it is a matter of showing a very great political will, and political commitment is most important. it is often said that more binding measures are needed. but we have to think. i have made a number of proposals which i believe are more intelligent than binding measures. but even the stability pact, which includes many binding measures, has not succeeded in bringing some countries back into line. so the method does not say everything, the method does not solve everything, the method without political commitment, without commitment is worth nothing at all. i am glad that some people say that more constraints are needed in the economic strategy. but the treaty of lisbon, for the economic guidelines, does not provide for this. i myself did not draw up the treaty of lisbon, others did, but it does not provide for sanctions, penalties or negative measures when it comes to the application of the economic guidelines. look closely at article 121 to be fully aware of it. political commitment at both european and national level is therefore crucial, and without this political commitment nothing will be achieved. one last word about greece. i think we got the message across. the message was that the greek government had a responsibility to deal with an extremely difficult situation, which it also inherited. he takes courageous action. he told us on 11 february that if the current measures were not sufficient to achieve a 4% reduction in the deficit in 2010, additional measures would be taken. we have committed ourselves to more monitoring not only at the initiative of the european commission but also with the help of the european central bank and even with the expertise of the international monetary fund. so i think we have really framed, delimited the responsibility aspect. there is of course, if necessary, an element of solidarity. greece has said that it does not want to use it, but we have two messages: a message of responsibility and a message of solidarity, if necessary. of course, we must draw conclusions from what has happened in greece in recent years. we need to be more proactive in both data collection and policy making in the euro area as well. this crisis was also a challenge, a challenge in the sense that we must put more effort into the policy of coordination. in fact, every crisis is a challenge. we must learn from every crisis. well, we'll pull them off. the lessons of the financial crisis should be learned from the lessons of the 1930s: more regulation, more control of bonuses, more prudent banking policy. but we must also learn all the lessons from the experience of greece and others. i believe, ladies and gentlemen, that i have felt the same ambition here, the same political will to pursue an economic policy, an economic strategy, which is commensurate with the difficulties we are facing today. we are indeed, as many of you have said - and this is not the responsibility of just one or two people - faced with a collective responsibility of all the european institutions and all the member states. if we do not, we cannot save our social model, or we will lose our position in the world. so it is with that spirit that i have come to meet you here this afternoon and it is with that spirit that i will continue my work. a situation which requires action, position or declaration by the united nations and the members of the united nations. in fact, the presidency of the european union, the presidency of the council, has always intervened systematically in the discussions of the various sessions of the human rights council on behalf of the european union, and that will continue to be the case. the presidency of the council of the union will be speaking at the next session of the human rights council on behalf of the council of the union; this is of course perfectly compatible with the statements and positions of each of the member states of the union and of the european commission, of course, as another institution of the union. i would therefore like to say that we are in favour of the existence of this body and in favour of the fact that all the possibilities can be drawn from it, which in some cases are achieved and in other cases are not: it is clear that there are certain situations in which, as a result of the votes that take place, the european union and its member states do not achieve all the objectives. there are some really positive cases, for example the position on somalia: there are human rights violations in that region; there are other cases where it has not been achieved. but it's always more the positive dimension side than the negative dimension side in this case. i would point out that, in connection with some of the cases of countries which have been mentioned in the various speeches, we are going to talk about some of them this afternoon. i would like to refer to the case of iran, because there have been repeated allusions to the issue of iran's candidacy. as you know, there have been statements constantly. i have before me, this year alone, three statements by the high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy, catherine ashton, on the situation in iran, condemning and expressing concern at some cases of human rights violations or executions that have taken place in iran. as regards the question of candidacy, we must first of all point out that we are dealing with a matter which is still a matter of national competence at the moment (the question of the position of the countries' candidacies to be members of the human rights council) and, in any case, that the management of the human rights situation in iran, the human rights violations that are taking place and, therefore, the eventual acceptance or rejection of iran's candidacy to the human rights council must be carried out, we understand, with caution so as not to generate effects contrary to the desired. that is why we believe that the european union should try to have as coordinated a position as possible in this field (which is what is happening at the moment), while respecting national competence and, as i say, with caution. in short, mr president, we believe that the human rights council is a place where we have to defend the position of the european union and that it is the right place to do so; moreover, our commitment to it has always been to ensure that there is no turning back, no turning back in the universal movement for the defence of human rights and, especially, that there is no turning back in a conquest of humanity, which is to consider human rights as a universal value, a universal value that must be defended beyond borders, beyond traditions and beyond diversities, because it is something that corresponds to the inner essence of human beings.

the problem of illegal immigration in greece is particularly acute in relation to the rest of the european union, mr president, as is well known. and the reasons are varied: from its geographical location to the vast extent of its maritime boundaries. under these circumstances, the greek government's initiative at this stage to facilitate the granting of greek citizenship to immigrants in an unprecedented way is at least tentative. and the paradox is that the proposal of the government of the country with the most acute problem includes the most lenient regulation, at every level, throughout the european union. in this way it encourages, rather than discourages, illegal immigration at the expense of legal immigration. it undermines social cohesion, it treats the issue piecemeal, dealing only with the last link in a chain that includes illegal entry, asylum, deportation, residence and work in the european union. and it opens the window to acquire european citizenship for an unspecified number of illegal immigrants. the commission's proposal is to be submitted to the council for approval, and the council will be able to accept it.

mr president, commissioner, mr fragueiro, the current common fisheries policy has failed. most fish stocks are collapsing. 88% of fish stocks are fished beyond the maximum sustainable level. 30% of fish stocks are outside safe biological limits, which means they have very low chances of recovery. the example of cod in the north sea is typical, caught even at ages before the breeding process begins. the amendment under discussion is therefore absolutely necessary. the protection of catches is a prerequisite for the protection of fishermen. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the fishing fleet is not depleted. the ecosystem approach should be the main principle of our new common fisheries policy, accompanied by long-term planning, participatory procedures and the application of the precautionary principle. this long-term approach to species conservation should be applied to all our international fisheries agreements. i would like to ask the commissioner to give us a clear indication of the extent to which the commission is prepared to take action in this area, and to give us the opportunity to make a statement on the matter.
mr president, i would also like to welcome commissioner damannakis and to thank in particular my colleague, mrs maria do céu patrão neves, for her exhaustive and excellent work. all the important things have already been said. i would like to focus on three points: one on overfishing. overfishing is an undeniable fact. in fact, as mr arsenis said, it is estimated today that up to 88% of the stocks in european seas are threatened by overfishing, that is to say, they are being fished to a degree that does not allow them to be renewed. overfishing over time has led to ever lower returns in european fisheries, with the loss of jobs. the fish caught are getting smaller, much before they are even of reproductive age, and they are getting harder to track. secondly, europe is catching far less fish today than it did 15 years ago - about 25% less - while, at the same time, fishing effort and costs have increased. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the fishing fleet is not over-exploited, and that the fishing fleet is not over-exploited. what we must not forget is that sustainability has three dimensions, as the neves report emphasizes: social, economic and ecological. a fisheries policy that aims at sustainable development must not only deal with fish but must also focus on people. fish, man, cormorants and seals are competing systems of the same ecological environment. finally, i should like to stress my determination, as several other colleagues have mentioned, to strengthen fisheries research. it is not my obsession, it is a reality that we must face in the context of what mr cadec said.
vice-president of the commission. − mr president, of course this discussion, now initiated by the tragic accident in belgium, will be part of our overall discussion on railway safety and the development of transport in europe. the commission is preparing a white paper on the future of transport which takes serious consideration of all safety and security aspects of all modes of transport, including railways – which is, as was mentioned many times, still one of the safest modes of transport. it is also important that we now discuss the railway package – the ‘first recast’ of the railway package – and we will definitely work on this and consider it. but i would just like to make some factual remarks. the european rail traffic management system (ertms) has been designed with the intention to have interoperability of railways. it is obviously a good system which has very serious safety elements. however, safety still remains the responsibility of member states, whatever system is used. but the ertms is progressing very well. transport ten-t networks: again we will discuss it soon. this particular project deals with the deployment of the traffic management system. by 2020, 20 000 kilometres of railways will use this system in europe, including belgium. this is ongoing; but in railways things take time and investments are large and 85% of the ten–t network money is used especially to improve the railways, including the ertms. of course i would be very happy if, with the support of the european parliament, we could increase the funding of investments to transport networks. that will be very important. but again, of course, the human factor is always relevant. and as we are talking about safety standards, there is one standard – which is the red light – that means that you must stop. that standard has existed since the 19th century. so if we are now saying that there will be a 100% sure braking system which avoids human error – it is not true. there is always some small possibility for human error. and human responsibility is very important. i would like to make one more remark about liberalisation and public services: these are two different things. nobody is stopping states from offering good public services, even in the framework of liberalisation. it is allowed by european rules to provide support – it is allowed by states – and this liberalisation does not exclude good public services.

in writing. the report supports the eu's common fisheries policy (cfp), which in the name of protecting fish stocks has led to the destruction of a large number of small fishing vessels in greece and the expulsion from the profession of many small and medium-sized fishermen, condemning many coastal areas to desertification and unemployment, concentrating activity in the hands of large fishing companies. the nature of the eu's pro-monopoly policy is shown by the fact that two thirds of the community funds went to big capital (fisheries, aquaculture, processing), while the remaining one third went to poor and middle-class fishermen to break up their boats and leave the profession. the measures to replace/improve vessels benefited only large companies. the report, like the green paper, equally assigns the responsibility for the decline in fish stocks to large fisheries and small-scale coastal fishing. it does not differentiate the measures required in fishing areas, ignoring their specific features. the eu's cfp serves the interests of the large fisheries companies that will be left to exploit the wealth of the sea and supports the large capital that is active in the aquaculture sector. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the fisheries sector is not left behind.
in writing. i voted against the report on the common fisheries policy, despite the fact that it contains some points which are a positive development in relation to the current situation. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of the marine environment is a very good one, and i would like to thank the rapporteur for the work he has done. the report fails to combine the necessary protection of the marine environment, the preservation of fish stocks and the social and economic protection of fishermen, particularly small-scale fishermen, with devastating consequences for the environment and sustainable fishing, harmful for fishermen and consumers who will also be burdened by the final price of the product, without this profit benefiting small fishermen but large private enterprises. the report fails to take account of the different circumstances in the individual countries of the union and therefore fails to provide the appropriate policies.

mr president, there is no doubt that the recent financial crisis has shown that the liberalisation of money markets and the obsession with free markets has allowed the financial system to grow dangerously in relation to and dependent on the real economy, as well as operating for years within a regime of huge profitability, uncertainty, without any regulation, which ultimately led to the crisis. the proposal for a financial transaction tax could therefore limit the size of the financial system and make certain speculative economic choices unworkable. it will be an empty letter, however, if this measure is not accompanied by a comprehensive plan for the regulation of the financial system, so as to limit to a minimum the abusive policies of the banks, the speculative games of the hedge funds and the rating agencies which today, in many countries, are aggravating and exploiting the fiscal problems. however, in my view, such a proposal should not be seen as a mere temporary measure. the banks should pay back the huge bailouts they received from european governments, which have resulted in a significant increase in their respective countries' budget deficits. these countries are now forced to borrow from the same banks and pay them back a second time. we need to be clear. banks must pay off their debts to the states. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them.
mr president, commissioner, the debate on the taxation of international financial transactions may not be new, but it has become particularly timely today because the main lesson of the crisis in the world economy, and in particular for the euro area, which has recently been subjected to systematic attacks by speculative capital, is that the lack of transparency in financial markets and the lack of effective financial regulation and governance has had a direct and visible impact on the real economy, the sustainability of public finances and social stability. in this context, the introduction of a tax on international financial transactions is of particular importance, as it is one of the key points of the long-awaited restructuring of financial control mechanisms. the solution, of course, is not to introduce another european tax with dubious consequences for the competitiveness of the european economy but to draw up an ambitious european proposal to be submitted to the g20.
mr president, commissioner, although developed countries are responsible for 80% of greenhouse gas emissions, developing countries are currently paying the worst of the consequences. the most dramatic effects are found in the poorest countries, in countries which have contributed nothing to the phenomenon. twenty million are today environmental, climate refugees. and if we don't do something right now, it's going to be five hundred million by 2050. so our climate debt to these countries is huge, and it's estimated at a hundred billion euros a year. of this, the european union's fair share is €35 billion. it is very important that we move immediately to tax financial transactions in order to be able to finance our climate debt. at the same time, this taxation allows us to restore intergenerational justice by paying off our climate debt to younger generations, helping to finance our energy decarbonization.

president of the commission. − as regards speculation, let us be clear that the current problems in greece were not caused by speculation. they were mainly caused by overspending and not respecting the european framework in terms of the stability and growth pact, namely the excessive debt, but it may happen afterwards that speculators act against the sovereign debt of that country. this also shows the importance of a fundamental reform in the derivatives market and the relevance of the action already undertaken by the commission. on 20 october 2009, the commission began a programme of action in favour of efficient, solid derivative markets. the legislative proposals that commissioner barnier will present before the summer, and also those concerning the market abuse directive that commissioner barnier will present before the end of the year, will increase market transparency and limit risks. beyond this systemic response, a new ad hoc reflection is needed on credit default swaps regarding sovereign debt, and the problem of ‘naked’ practices needs particular attention in this context. it is not justified to buy insurance and buy unseen interventions on a risk on a purely speculative basis. in the short term, we must achieve the necessary coordination to ensure that member states act in a coordinated fashion, but most particularly for naked practices. in this context, the commission will examine closely the relevance of banning purely speculative naked sales of credit default swaps for sovereign debt. at the same time, we will push for international coordination. because these markets are opaque, we are going to bring this issue to the g20 and we also have to raise some of these issues in our bilateral contacts, particularly with the united states.

heritage. the commission shall promote cultural cooperation between creators, cultural operators and institutions in the countries participating in the programme with a view to encouraging the development of european citizenship. the culture programme aims in particular to promote the transnational mobility of cultural operators, to encourage the transnational circulation of artists and cultural works and products and to support intercultural dialogue. as an illustration, in 2009, 749 applications were submitted under the culture programme and 256 projects were selected for funding, independent contractor to assess the first three years of implementation of the culture 2007-2009 programme and, in particular, the programme's relevance to objectives, first results and initial impact. the evaluation shall be carried out by the contractor on the basis of data on the results of projects, recent individual evaluations, surveys and interviews with project beneficiaries and cultural operators concerned. the final report will be submitted in the second half of this year. on this basis, the commission will draw up a report on the implementation of the programme and submit
