mr president, i voted against the report because the european union 2020 strategy is following the same failed neoliberal path as the lisbon strategy, which has led to the widening of regional and social inequalities, the increase in poverty and unemployment and has been a major cause of the crisis in the european union. the economic and social policy framework must therefore be radically changed to focus on full employment and the strengthening of social rights. the european union leaders in the informal council, when the crisis broke out, hid away, leaving each state to deal with the problems on its own, and now they are coming to monitor budget deficits. they have treated greece as the black sheep and are seeking to take tough measures to the detriment of the workers of greece and other countries. the european parliament has already expressed its concern about the situation in the former yugoslavia, and we are therefore calling for the immediate withdrawal of the troops from the country.
mr. president, thank you for your patience. i voted against the report because it repeats the dangerous directives given by the treaty of lisbon on the european defence and security strategy. it is calling for the militarization of the european union, it is legitimizing military interventions, it is recognizing nato's primacy and its close relationship with it, and it is even pushing for an increase in military spending, especially in times of crisis and great social needs. in my view, the european union must, more than ever, at a time when the architecture of the world is being judged, pursue a peace-loving policy and a different political conception of security, pursue an independent foreign and defence policy, freed from the united states, seek to settle international disputes by political means and take the lead in respecting international law and the enhanced role of the united nations. i think that this policy is the best way of expressing the european citizen.
in writing. i voted in favour of the lehne report, as it gives member states the discretion to take account of the different effects that the implementation of the directive may have within their own member states, in particular as regards the number of undertakings covered by it. the commission has also proposed that the member states should be allowed to apply the principle of subsidiarity to the activities of micro-organisms. in addition, the publication of annual accounts ensures transparency and is a necessary condition for access to the financial market, public procurement and inter-company relations for micro-enterprises.
in writing. i voted against the second part of paragraph 6 of the joint resolution on the ee 2020 strategy, as it suggests a proposal to further weaken the traditionally structured european welfare state. the eu should make its social union more visible by countering the competitive pressure in the international economic arena from forces that have either made a visible deforestation of social benefits and structures or are engaged in social dumping. it seems that social and employment policy is selectively and flexibly adapted to market dynamics. the integration strategy tends to claim institutional completeness in relation to market forces, but it is imperfect in the political regulation of effects and phenomena of disintegration (e.g. unemployment, regional inequalities, lack of social cohesion). the signs of the times call more than ever for a more social europe.
in writing. the joint resolution of the social democratic and liberal people's party on the eu strategy "europe 2020" expresses the common decision of the political staff of capital to implement by all means the savage attack and anti-people plans of the monopolies against the working class, the workers throughout the eu. the europe 2020 strategy continues and deepens the anti-people "lisbon strategy", defining the strategic objectives and plans of monopoly capital, as it puts in the cradle of progress fundamental wage and social rights of workers, and in particular: generalized application of the notorious "well-being" in combination with "lifelong learning", "training and retraining" and "mobility" of workers, abolition of the s.s. of labour, rotation of work, drastic reduction of wages and pensions, increase of the retirement age and in general sweeping changes in social security, health, welfare, education. it also provides capital with plenty of money from the state funds in the form of subsidies and incentives in the name of "green growth". the committee also welcomes the commission's proposal to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of the term 'competent authority' to cover all the activities of the commission.
in writing. the european parliament's report on the eu's common foreign and security policy, together with the corresponding report on the european security and defence policy, produced by the anti-people coalition of conservatives, social democrats and liberals in the european parliament, reflects the firm support of political expressions of capital for the promotion of even greater militarisation of the eu, especially after the entry into force of the reactionary lisbon treaty, as well as their active role in promoting the eu's imperialist policy, interventions and wars waged against third countries and peoples in every country on the planet, to serve the interests of the imperialist domination and the conditions of monopoly competition, in conditions of capitalist domination. the report calls for: (a) the effective organisation of the eu's european external action service (established by the treaty of lisbon), this new political-military arm for organising, supporting and executing the eu's imperialist interventions; · (b) an increase in expenditure from the eu budget for its military and political interventions; (c) a better integration of the eu's political and military capabilities, with the key point being the strengthening of the eu-nato interface, in order to carry out its imperialist interventions by military means more effectively. the committee of the regions condemns this unacceptable report, which can only be described as a manual of imperialist attacks on peoples.
in writing. the european parliament's report on the eu's csdp is a call for a generalised war by the eu's imperialist centre against the people. it marks a new intensification of competition with the other centres of imperialism. the report: it welcomes the 70,000 members of the eu's 23 military and civilian missions around the world, in most cases in cooperation with the us and nato. it welcomes the imperialist naval surveillance of somalia by eu naval forces. the european parliament calls on the eu to set up a 'state mechanism', a coastguard and a regular army for sudan abroad, but not to overthrow the government of the country. supports the 'establishment of a civilian-military crisis management and planning directorate' and the 'creation of a permanent union operations centre'. calls for an intensification of state terrorism and the strangulation of democratic rights in the name of 'combating terrorism' and 'radicalisation' it promotes the rapid organisation of the european external action service with politico-military responsibilities. the european union is also calling for the establishment of a european union-wide military and political intervention force, in the framework of the so-called mutual assistance provided for in the 'solidarity clause' of the lisbon treaty. the only interest of the peoples is to break with the whole of the imperialist and anti-people policy and the very structure of the eu.
in writing. i consider it of the utmost priority and importance to strengthen efforts against the proliferation of nuclear weapons, towards a world free of nuclear weapons. this includes strengthening the treaty on the non-proliferation of nuclear weapons (npt) through its signature and implementation by all member states. i have chosen to abstain on this resolution because it contains a key point which i am opposed to and which the left group has tried, unsuccessfully, to change. i refer to the wording and substance of the view that the eu can 'use all the means at its disposal to prevent, deter, halt and, if possible, eliminate dissemination programmes', which creates serious problems. in particular, the use or threat of use of war and military means, especially with regard to iran, is not only extremely dangerous, will not have positive effects on peace, but also runs counter to the left's view of the eu's military actions and actions.
welcome, high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy. the arctic is the part of the planet where climate change is most pronounced. global warming has led to a significant retreat of the ice. a milestone year was 2007, when ice declined by 34% compared to the 1970-2000 period. but the melting of the arctic ice has many, many dramatic consequences. it leads to accelerated climate change. until now, the white surface of the arctic ice has reflected 80 percent of the sunlight that falls on the region, affecting global and local temperatures. this reflection is steadily decreasing as the temperature of the planet and the wider polar region increases over a 1,500-meter zone within canada, russia, and alaska. in fact, in 2007, between august and october, there was a 2°c increase in temperature. at the same time, melting ice is causing unpredictable changes in ocean currents. it negatively affects marine ecosystems, fisheries, and reduces the ability of the sea to absorb carbon dioxide, as it affects plankton and other organisms, and raises sea levels. for this reason, mr high representative, european citizens are saddened by the european union's often discussed participation in the escalating competition for geopolitical benefits from this environmental disaster in the arctic. the role of the european union should not be to win an international geopolitical contest over oil and arctic shipping lanes. our role should be to ensure that our principles are respected, that the environmental integrity of the region is respected, that principles such as international cooperation prevail, that the un institutions are respected in any new regime that emerges in the arctic from this enormous environmental disaster.

in writing. the resolution concerns the draft council decision supplementing the schengen borders code on the surveillance of maritime borders in the context of operations coordinated by frontex for rescue measures at sea. as regards greece, and in view of the increasing migratory pressures, these measures facilitate the presence of frontex in the greek maritime area. in particular, these measures consist of both rules and non-binding guidelines and focus on the reception, search and rescue of people at sea. in substance, these are measures to be taken in the event that a ship is spotted and there is a suspicion that persons are on board trying to escape border control. in addition, search and rescue should be carried out on the basis of specific principles and the disembarkation of persons apprehended or rescued should be carried out on the basis of a specific operational plan. i therefore believe that this initiative should be supported and that the measures referred to in the council resolution should be implemented more quickly.

mr president, canada is one of the oldest and closest allies of the european union, dating back to 1959. however, our cooperation must always be based on shared values and mutual respect. canada is among the top ten greenhouse gas polluters in the world and is the only country that signed and ratified the kyoto protocol and then publicly announced that it has no intention of honoring its legal commitments. instead of reducing its emissions by 6% compared to 1990, canada's emissions increased by 26%. oil sands production is the main cause. the greenhouse gas emissions from oil sands production are 3 to 5 times higher than conventional oil and gas production. oil sand production also requires two to five barrels of water for every barrel of tar that is exported, and then creates a series of wastes that threaten both biodiversity and the lives of the indigenous people. production also destroys the boreal forest, one of the largest carbon reservoirs on the planet. by 2020, oil sands will probably produce more emissions than austria and ireland. canada spends only $77 per person on green grants, while korea spends $1,200, australia $420, and the us $365. ensuring the protection of the boreal forest is very important, and it is important to ask canada to comply with the international agreements we have jointly signed, but only we respect unilaterally, and this should be the basis for any further cooperation.

functioning of the economy and the financial markets. the rating agencies play a leading role in assessing the risks of the situation of companies, as indeed in the situation of states, and the crisis has shown that their operation, to say the least, has posed and poses problems with sometimes very heavy consequences. that is why the g20 has rightly taken strong decisions to put in place supervision and new governance rules. i would like to remind you, ladies and gentlemen, that at the time of the crisis the commission very quickly took up its responsibilities in this area and made the regulation of the activities of credit rating agencies a priority over the last two years. as early as september 2009, one year after lehman's bankruptcy, the regulation on credit rating agencies was adopted with the support of the european parliament. i pay tribute here in particular to the work of your rapporteur, mr gauzès, in addressing the problems raised by the way these agencies operated, which contributed significantly to the financial crisis. the regulation i am referring to introduced a mandatory registration regime for all credit rating agencies established in the european union. it has imposed a series of stringent requirements, first to ensure that potential conflicts of interest are eliminated, second to review and enhance the quality of ratings and the methodology for rating, and third to ensure that these rating agencies act in a transparent manner. ladies and gentlemen, i am confident that the new rules on credit rating agencies that i have just mentioned will decisively improve the independence and integrity of the credit rating process and will enhance the transparency of credit rating activities and the quality of credit ratings, including those relating to the sovereign debt of states, european union countries and financial institutions in the union. so here we are. as regards the creation of a european public credit rating agency, as you wish, mr papastamkos, this idea is part of the debate on possible alternatives to the current business model of credit rating agencies, which is a so-called 'issuer-payer' model. the effects of such an idea must be carefully assessed, particularly in terms of liability. clearly, mr. member, my first priority today is to ensure that the 2009 regulation is properly implemented and that the current, renewed system is operational. but i am not closing the door on the idea that you support of the creation of a european agency. this has to be considered in the light of the assessment of the 2009 regulation and its effects on the rating agencies. moreover, this evaluation is provided for in the regulation and the commission must submit it to your parliament and the council by december 2012. what i can confirm is that the commission will soon propose an amendment to the regulation on credit rating agencies to give the new european financial market authority, esma, overall responsibility for the supervision of these agencies. you, the european parliament, asked for this when negotiating the regulation, and the heads of state agreed on this principle. so we're going to do it. i am convinced that the transfer of the supervision of credit rating agencies to the new authority will strengthen and improve the regulatory framework we have in our european union.

member of the commission. − indicators reveal that over the last decade there has been a disconnection between wage and productivity developments in greece. this has generated competitiveness losses, reflected in persistent current account deficits and a fall in export market shares. labour market rigidities and wage-setting have been identified as an important factor behind the excessive wage growth in greece and the resulting gap in unit labour costs with its main trading partners. in recent years, domestic demand has been the main contributor to economic growth, fuelled by buoyant growth in general government expenditure and household incomes. private final consumption expenditure per capita increased by more than 80% over the last decade. this model has clearly been unsustainable, resulting in the build-up of significant fiscal, which means a high general government deficit and growth debt stock, increasing interest payments and macroeconomic, which implies a high current account deficit and external debt outflow of income imbalances. the increased financing needs of the government have resulted in the public sector absorbing a large part of the available financing, thus ruling out the private sector and adversely affecting the economy’s growth prospects. economy-wide wage moderation, with public sector wage cuts playing an important signalling role to the private sector, and fiscal austerity measures are thus indispensable to put the greek economy on a stronger footing by restoring competitiveness and achieving fiscal consolidation. the commission is aware that fiscal austerity measures and wage moderation may have a negative short-term impact on demand. nonetheless, given the current situation that greece is facing, these measures are necessary to restore market confidence and to lay down the foundations for a more sustainable growth model for the greek economy in the long term. greece has adopted an ambitious programme to correct its deficit and to reform its public administration and the economy. the consolidation measures taken by greece are important for enhancing fiscal sustainability and market confidence and have been strongly welcomed by the commission, the eurogroup, the european central bank and the international monetary fund. the courageous measures included in the stability programme and the packages announced in february and march 2010 include not only the envisaged wage cuts through a reduction in allowances paid to civil servants and easter, summer and christmas bonuses, but also measures to improve the tax collection mechanism, widen the tax base and increase tax compliance. in the communication adopted on 9 march 2010, the commission concluded that greece is implementing the council question no 38 by mr gay mitchell (h-0145/10) subject: the situation in the former yugoslavia the idea of a european monetary fund has been raised in recent weeks as a mechanism for dealing with crises such as the one that struck greece earlier this year. what is the situation with regard to this proposal? how could such a fund function in practical terms? what are the main obstacles to the creation of an enp? for example, is it possible to create it on the basis of the provisions of the present treaty?
member of the commission. − the crisis has demonstrated the need for establishing a crisis resolution framework for the euro area. due to the need to consider all economic, legal and institutional implications, this is an issue for the medium term rather than the immediate view. the heads of state and governments of the euro area gave a strong signal on 25 march, by calling for the establishment of a task force to work on measures for the euro-area framework for crisis resolution before the end of the year. the public discussion regarding a european monetary fund has touched a number of elements that are relevant in this respect. in particular, the commission agrees that there is a case for establishing a framework for emergency financial support under strict conditionality and subject to incentive-compatible interest rates. however, no new body is needed to provide it or to define and monitor conditionality. consistency with the stability-oriented governance framework of the emu needs to be ensured. the commission is considering the scope of proposals to this effect. more generally, a firm commitment to sound policies by all euro-area member states remains the cornerstone of the successful functioning of the emu. in this context, the commission is in the process of preparing for the proposals on reinforced economic policy coordination and country surveillance building on the proposals presented in the recent commission communication on europe 2020 strategy.
member of the commission. − you should put the question on a specific time-frame to commission rehn, but when you look at the recommendations that we have been making and the agreement that has been made to support greece, in particular, by a combination of bilateral loans and international monetary fund support, it is clear that the commission is of the opinion that what happened now in any case could not be resolved by the putting into place of a european monetary fund because this would certainly take much more time than we have with respect to greece. so this is a medium-term project that we are sympathetic with, but with respect to a specific time-frame, i really suggest you put the question to mr rehn.

governance. a forthcoming communication will outline new proposals in order to frame the development of a comprehensive framework for crisis prevention and correction in the euro area through recourse to the new article 136 of the treaty on the functioning of the european union. the communication may include proposals to reinforce the preventive and corrective arms of the stability and growth pact; proposals for more effective and broader surveillance of intra-euro area macroeconomic imbalances and explore the options for the creation of a crisis resolution mechanism for euro-area countries. times. underlying vulnerabilities of public finances should be taken properly into account when designing the optimal consolidation part. new focus should be given to debt dynamics and sustainability imbalances and competitiveness diversions are particularly warranted for eu member states that linked to the euro because of the higher degree of economic and financial spillovers across euroarea member states; less market discipline; the absence of exchange rate risks and more challenging adjustment with potentially high cost for the euro area as a whole. competitiveness divergences are a cause of serious concern for the functioning of the european monetary union. during the decade preceding the crisis, divergence has been underpinned by a worrying build-up of a range of domestic increased vulnerability of public finances. at the same time, countries heavily relying on trade surpluses have fallen victim to the sharp contraction in world trade in the early stages of the global crisis. therefore, complementing fiscal surveillance, the commission intends coming forward with proposals for the broadening of economic surveillance in the euro area, addressing macroeconomic imbalances and competitive developments. the aim is to set up a framework for early detection, prevention and effective correction of intra-euro area imbalances. the third main element in the commission’s proposal will explore the options for setting up a crisis resolution mechanism. the ad hoc mechanism for possible financial assistance for greece serves the immediate need. however, it is provision of exceptional and conditional support for a euro-area country in serious distress will bolster the fundaments of the emu. the proposals for enhanced economic surveillance and coordination in the euro area are an important complement to the eu’s comprehensive 2020 strategy for growth and jobs. the commission will ensure the efficient articulation between the two frameworks.

fayot has referred to: what measures should be taken. it seems to me that the debate we have had on swift can shed some light on this. i think the principles we have talked about, the principles we have agreed on, should be present here. we are talking about the rights to privacy, the rights to intimacy, the rights to personality, to self-image, which must always be preserved. fundamental rights are indivisible and in this case we are dealing with something which could violate fundamental rights and i think we must act with the same care as we have spoken about in the previous debate. and finally, a third consideration i should like to make in connection with the foregoing. as a general reflection, it does not seem to me that security and freedom are two opposing principles, that is to say, that it is a kind of zero-sum game and that, to the extent that we give more security, we will have less freedom, or to the extent that we protect more fundamental rights and freedoms and are fundamentalists in the protection of fundamental rights, we will have less security. i think this is a false dilemma. i believe that security and freedom are two principles which reinforce each other and both principles are therefore expressed and recognised as principles which form part of the constitutions, of european laws and are also both present in the treaty of lisbon. i would like to ask the commissioner whether he is aware that the commission has not yet taken a decision on the matter. we therefore believe that when we look beyond the short term, because we sometimes act with a strong short-term bias, and think in the long term, measures to protect our security will always prove to be prudent and reasonable, and effective, and the protection of rights and freedoms will always contribute to the well-being and ultimately even to the security of citizens.

member of the commission. − madam president, honourable members, my colleague, commissioner piebalgs excuses himself. unfortunately he cannot be here with you today, so he has entrusted me with the task of taking this debate with you. thank you for this opportunity to explain the commission’s position on the use of cyanide for gold extraction in the european union. first, as the honourable member knows, we have had a careful and very comprehensive study of the dramatic accident and the causes of it at baia mare in romania in 2000 when a dam retaining toxic substances broke. the conclusions of that study were taken on board when the european union adopted in 2006 a specific directive on the management of extracted waste. the deadline for member states to transpose this was only two years ago and it is still regarded as an up-to-date, proportionate and appropriate approach to the risk of using cyanide. the directive includes several requirements to improve the safety of extractive waste management facilities and limit their impact on the environment. explicit and precise requirements are set on the construction and the management of waste facilities which have to be operated using the ‘best available technique’ concept. a full accident prevention policy is required for the facilities in which toxic substances are treated or stored. emergency plans to be used in case of accidents must be established, not only by the operator but also by the competent authorities. clear information requirements are included in the directive if trans-boundary impacts are expected. this legislation also incorporates requirements for the closure of extraction facilities, and for after closure. it includes the obligation to set up an underwritten financial guarantee for each installation before the beginning of the operation. the directive includes strict maximum limit values of cyanide concentration before this substance is stored in ponds for remaining residues to be broken down by oxidation, sunlight or bacteria. in practice, in order to meet the strict limit values, it is necessary to install specific equipment destroying most of the cyanide before its storage in the pond. to our best knowledge, unfortunately, no adequate alternatives to cyanide use for gold extraction exist on the market. in most european deposits, gold is bound with other metals meaning that a separation method is required. a total cyanide ban would imply stopping european extraction and consequently increase gold imports, often from countries with lower environmental and social standards. nevertheless, the commission is following technology development in the sector and, if alternative techniques emerge in the coming years, the debate might very well be reopened. in the mean time, a good implementation of this directive is essential to guarantee the safety of these facilities and minimise the risk associated with their management. let me also point out that member states are responsible for deciding on whether to open gold mines on their territories. the commission’s role is to ensure full implementation of the directive and good implementation and enforcement is a priority. under the directive, the member states are bound to provide the commission with information on implementation no later than 2012 and we in turn are obliged to analyse and report on this basis. that will obviously be the right time for us to assess the effectiveness of this approach and if, at that point, the current approach were found to be ineffective, we should not rule out the possibility of an outright ban. in conclusion, i would like to insist on the importance of ensuring high waste-recycling rates and improved resource efficiency in the extraction sector. even without considering the use of cyanide, mining for gold is far from kind to the environment. to extract 1 g of gold it is necessary to move and treat, on average, 5 000 kg of ore. the same amount can be obtained through the recycling of approximately 5 kg of old mobile phones. this example illustrates the importance of increasing the separate collection and recycling of waste – in this case electronic and electrical waste which can contain gold and other similar precious metals. this is why resource efficiency is a priority for this commission.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. madam president, this is a very important subject to discuss, because it is a very dangerous material, cyanide. we do not accept what we have heard from the commission spokesman, that there are no non-dangerous techniques. we believe that in greece, since there are three investment projects in the mining of gold with cyanide, they should be dealt with by banning this technique. in evros, rhodes, halkidiki there is a strong reaction from the local communities and there are also decisions from the country's supreme administrative court, the council of state. the threat of the international monetary fund being involved in the crisis in my country raises fears of possible pressure and relaxation of environmental legislation and controls. there are practices and experiences from other countries with tragic results. in greece, the risks also come from the exploitation of gold in bulgaria, which is in the evros watershed. there is also the question of the turkish coast and the related threats to the aegean. similar schemes exist in other countries. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's energy policy is not undermined by the fact that the community is not able to meet its own needs. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the european union's financial instruments are not used to the detriment of the people of the union. we call for the weak european union legislation to be made more decisive and for there to be no more different levels of permitted pollutants per member state.
the commission is therefore proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the following areas: the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full, and i am sure that the commission will take the necessary steps to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. the commission and the attitude it has taken is lax, the directive is permeable, it does not prevent the dangers to which other colleagues have referred. the importance and impact of the use of cyanide in the mining of metals is well known, and we have the example of romania. the honourable member referred to mining projects currently being developed in greece. in my question to the commission on the establishment of a cyanide gold mine in bulgaria, the commission's reply reinforced my fears and the need for this legislation to be made stricter and its implementation more decisive. we are sure that the citizens will obviously react, but we must also act. we therefore join our voice with all those who call for a total ban on the use of cyanide in the extraction of precious metals, and all countries should, as hungary recently did, commit themselves to this ban.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the nuclear safety of the community is not compromised. but in 2000 the second greatest environmental disaster in the history of europe - and perhaps the world - was caused by the baia mare accident in romania, which many colleagues have mentioned. 100,000 cubic meters of water with very high concentrations of cyanide and other heavy metals leaked from a gold mining plant into the tisla river and thence into the danube, affecting all but romania, hungary and serbia, killing tens of thousands of fish and poisoning drinking water. the contamination of the food chain in the directly affected areas has been longstanding. hungary reported 1,367 tonnes of dead fish. over 100 people, mostly children, were poisoned and immediately hospitalized after eating the contaminated fish. however, gold mining using cyanide solutions not only continues, not only is it not prohibited at european level, but the investments involved are subsidized by the member states and the european union. mining is ongoing or planned to start in sweden, finland, slovakia, romania, bulgaria and greece, while it is prohibited by law in hungary, the czech republic and by case law in germany. the time has now passed when we exchanged jobs at the expense of the local environment and the health of the citizens. the economic viability of this activity would also collapse if we were to apply the principle of prevention and the polluter pays principle. any economic activity is welcome, provided it is compatible with the protection of the environment and the health of citizens. but when we use cyanide, we put the environment and the health of the citizens at irreparable risk. commissioner malmström, can you assure us that we have sufficient and strong legislation and that a new baia mare will not be repeated this time in sweden, finland, bulgaria or greece? i would ask the commission to show that it is honouring the commitments it made to the european parliament just two months ago. i join the voices of the local communities who suffer the most and the struggles of the environmental movements in calling for an immediate ban on the use of cyanide in gold mining within the european union.
madam president, madam commissioner, the gold is there, it will not escape. the question of when, by what technique and with what environmental impact we will decide to mine it is what we are called upon to discuss. if a cyanide deposit is used, the effects are irreversible, because the gold is gone and the deposits of cyanide-containing dangerous toxic substances, as the directive itself states, remain in large quantities in the mining area. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's fishing fleet is not disrupted by the introduction of new fishing vessels. the current directive has one drawback: the financial guarantee provided does not cover all the effects in the event of an accident, in particular after the closure of the installations concerned. the basic principle of 'the polluter pays' is therefore violated, especially since the companies using this technique are mainly non-european and when the extraction is over, they wave the handkerchief and leave. there should therefore be a serious review of alternative extraction methods and a re-establishment of the basic 'polluter pays' principle with full and reliable insurance cover in the event of an accident, now and for as long as these dangerous substances remain trapped in the earth. as long as these conditions are not met, i believe that there should be a complete ban on this technology, which will perhaps also give incentives for companies to seriously investigate alternative, less polluting techniques, because if you have a cheap method that you do not pay for its pollution, you have no reason to investigate the alternatives.

in writing. the positive vote on the europeana programme means support for the effort to digitize the cultural heritage of the european countries. it is, however, very important to note that the aim is to protect the actual electronic form of the works without giving the user the possibility of modifying them. in short, the aim is not to develop another internet search engine but a site that will be both a museum, a library and a source of scientific knowledge. the digitisation of cultural heritage, however, cannot be achieved without the help of the member states and national bodies. unfortunately, today 47% of europeana's content comes from france, while countries that should have a strong presence given their rich cultural heritage, such as greece, represent only a small percentage of the digitized archives. in addition, particular attention should be paid to the protection of copyright. digitalisation means free access for citizens to knowledge and science and in no case a new field of action for cyber piracy and hacking.
in writing. the new digital agenda for europe is a very optimistic programme for the dissemination of new technologies and fast connections in the member states and that is why i voted in favour of it. however, beyond the enlightening principles it expresses, such as increasing mobile speeds and familiarizing citizens with new technologies, some goals seem particularly difficult to achieve. in particular, the target that all schools in the european union should have high-speed internet by 2015, while highly desirable, seems difficult to achieve due to objective factors (for example, in isolated mountain and island countries, high speeds are difficult to achieve immediately). the new european agenda for digitisation should therefore be supported as soon as possible by a series of coordinated actions and initiatives, such as more generous community funding, to ensure better internet access even for students who are geographically disadvantaged.
in writing. the liberadzki report 'on the discharge in respect of the implementation of the general budget of the european union for the financial year 2008, section iii commission and executive agencies' adopts particularly negative characteristics for greece on a number of issues ranging from the distortion of fiscal statistics to the indefinite classification of the country as having general corruption. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. however, this was not possible and that is why i voted against the liberadzki report as a whole.
in writing. i voted against this resolution because it does not reject the massive exchange of data with the united states and other countries in the context of the so-called fight against terrorism. it also fails to promote the need for an international binding agreement between the eu and the us on the framework for exchange of information for law enforcement purposes. finally, while the european parliament must give its consent to the proposed agreement, it is unacceptable that negotiations, however informal, should have been launched without its full and equal participation.
in writing. the european union is also committed to the principle of subsidiarity, which is the basis for the european union's policy on the environment. the aim of parliament is to set out the minimum rules for promoting transatlantic cooperation leading to the fight against terrorism and the creation of a transmission system that can be trusted by the citizens of the union. one of the most sensitive points of the negotiations, to which particular attention must be paid, is the reduction in the volume of data transferred. to achieve this, the new agreement should include a series of safeguards aimed at respecting european legislation on the protection of personal data of european citizens. the resolution also stresses the importance of providing eu citizens with a better mechanism for appealing to courts to protect their rights more effectively.
in writing. the creation of a single model for passenger statuses to be applied to pnr agreements with all the countries concerned and the postponement of the vote on the request for approval of the agreements with the usa and australia appear to be the best possible solution. a hasty approach leading to a possible no vote on the pnr agreements with the usa and australia would have the effect of stopping the flow of data and perhaps this would mean cancellation of landing rights with disastrous consequences for the air carriers. the joint resolution tabled today by all the groups in parliament, which i also supported, rightly states that pnr agreements must take account of minimum standards which are not subject to negotiation. the safety of passengers is a paramount objective, but this cannot be achieved at the expense of respect for their privacy and the protection of their personal data. the collection of passenger data in a restricted manner is of paramount importance for the transmission of passenger data and should always be based on the principle of proportionality and necessity.
in writing. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the use of cyanide in the mining industry is not restricted to the production of cyanide, but that it is also used in the production of other products. the commission has so far taken a very lax approach to this matter and this must change immediately. the issue concerns many countries, the health of european citizens and the protection of the environment. the cases and history of the consequences of the use of cyanide in metallurgy, as has occurred in romania and other countries, are well known and cause for concern. the commission's reply to my question on the recent decision to set up a cyanide-based gold mine in bulgaria has increased our fears. unfortunately, the use of cyanide seems possible at the moment in northern greece with three investment projects by foreign companies. finally, the commission must propose a complete ban on the use of cyanide in the eu within the next six months, with a view to implementing it by the end of 2012 at the latest. the commission has also proposed that the council should adopt a directive on the use of cyanide in the manufacture of certain products.

acting president of the council. - mr president, i should like to begin by answering the direct question put to me by mr bokros. mr cofferati, who is not in the chamber at the moment, has also referred to this, as has mrs del castillo, who is not in the chamber either. other people have referred to it. why has the lisbon strategy failed? that was the direct question mr bokros asked. well, i think there are probably many reasons and it would be a bit excessive and arrogant to want to simplify it, but if i had to choose one of those reasons, it seems to me that the most definitive explanation for this lack of success in the lisbon strategy is that the european union - which approved the single market at the time, which approved a single currency - has not taken that step which needs to be taken towards economic union. that step has not been taken. the maastricht treaty spoke of economic and monetary union. we have stayed in monetary union, we have not moved to economic union. and that is why i believe that the europe 2020 strategy must be inscribed precisely in a new stage of the union, which is the step towards economic union. economic union means, first and foremost, economic and social governance of the union. a fundamental element of this economic union is a strategy for growth and the creation of quality jobs, which is essentially the subject of this debate; a debate which, moreover, i found very interesting and extremely rich in contributions and which also has new, important dimensions that were not in the lisbon strategy, or not with that emphasis. for example, the technological or social dimension referred to by mr cofferati, mr cercas and mr arif, and a dimension of combating climate change, which i link to what mrs schroedter said. not only that, but it is possible to achieve economic union by having a strategy of growth and quality job creation. not only that. and with that i would reply to mrs harms, who is not present in this chamber. because there is also something missing which commissioner olli rehn - who will speak next - is working on and which i referred to earlier. we need a coordination of economic, employment and social policies which has not been achieved in europe and which was not achieved with the lisbon strategy. and it is something that the treaty of lisbon obliges us to do. article 5 of the treaty on the functioning of the european union states that the member states of the union must, are obliged - not have the power - to coordinate their economic and employment policies. and they could also, if they wished - in my view they should - coordinate their social policies. in addition to this, in addition to a strategy for growth and job creation and in addition to coordination of economic and employment policies, we need european supervision of the financial markets, and that is the supervision package to which i referred earlier and to which i had a reply from mr verhofstadt. i am very glad that he is in favour of parliament adopting his position on the financial supervision package as soon as possible. and, in addition to that, something that mr barroso has particularly emphasized in his speech: we need to have an external dimension. europe's economic union must have an external dimension, a single position towards the outside, namely the g20. i refer to the words of mr barroso, with which i agree almost entirely. and in order to have an economic union, we also need governance institutions: a european council that sets the strategic lines, a commission that monitors, monitors and implements this strategy, and legislative bodies for this strategy: the council and the european parliament. and, in addition, instruments to give a positive incentive to this strategy, such as the authorization of the structural funds and european funds to guide this strategy, something which has not exactly happened, or at least not very much, during the years of the lisbon strategy. this is what i believe is already under way in the european union: a step towards the next stage, the one required by the 21st century, the stage of globalisation, which is economic union. not just the internal market, not just monetary union, but economic union too. that is the way we must go, and we must do so consistently, with interinstitutional dialogue, as is happening here this afternoon, and with the utmost speed. i believe that this is what all of us citizens of europe are asking for.

acting president of the council. - madam president, today in athens three people have lost the first human right, which is life. it has been the result of violent acts which we condemn absolutely, categorically. the spanish presidency of the council, on behalf of the council, wishes to express its condolences and sympathy to the families and therefore supports the statement made by the president of this parliament. we are talking about human rights, accession to the european convention for the protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms, one of which, as i said, is the right to life and physical integrity. the european union is founded on human rights and freedoms and throughout its existence, in the texts that have been adopted, there has been a constant reference to fundamental rights and freedoms. the treaty of lisbon is the culmination of this. the lisbon treaty, on the one hand, incorporates for the first time in european history a legally binding charter of fundamental rights of the citizens of europe and, on the other hand, tells the institutions that the union will be party to the european convention for the protection of human rights. we are therefore witnessing the culmination of a political, cultural and legal journey of the union on human rights, which the union places at the heart of its policies, at the heart of its action, at the heart of its personality. in this context, it seems to us of the utmost importance that the european union has already started the procedure for being able to sign the european convention for the protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms in due course, which means, among other things, accepting the jurisdiction of the strasbourg court of human rights; and means increasing the guarantees for citizens and, so to speak, a kind of rapprochement, convergence between the systems of human rights and freedoms that coexist in europe: the national systems - the guarantees that exist in each european country, which are democratic countries that respect and defend human rights - the european union's system and the european convention for the protection of human rights, which is another legal system to which not only the members of the european union but also other european countries, even if they are not part of the union, belong. we are therefore witnessing a process of convergence of these legal systems and the expression of this will be the signing of this convention by the european union. on 17 march the commission presented a recommendation to open negotiations for the union's accession to the convention. and the council has since done its utmost to speed up the discussions on the negotiating mandate. there is a working group in the council which is developing these discussions in close cooperation with the european commission. the council has taken very much into account all the mandates contained in protocol 8, which is the legal reference in this respect. for example, the possible participation of the union in the control bodies of the european convention or the need to respect the union's competences and the powers of the institutions. the need to appoint a european union judge to the court in due course, the involvement of this parliament in the parliamentary assembly of the council of europe, and also the union's involvement in the committee of ministers when it exercises functions relating to the application of the european convention on human rights. the council has also followed very closely the debates and hearings held by this european parliament in march this year and is taking very much into account the views expressed by the european parliament in the draft report drawn up by the rapporteurs, mr ramón jáuregui atondo, mr kinga gál and mr cristian dan preda. the spanish presidency's forecast, the council's position, is that the mandate for negotiations with the european council, which will be time-consuming and of a technical and complex nature, will be adopted before the end of the first half of 2010.
vice-president of the commission. − madam president, my colleague olli rehn has already expressed the position and the condolences of the commission concerning the greek disaster, so let me just look at how we can advance with our work because this will be of the utmost importance for completing the system of protection of fundamental rights within the union, and the accession of the eu to the european convention on human rights, which is enshrined in the lisbon treaty, is not an option. it is a destination, as the presidency so well expressed it just now, but this accession is only one of the four elements of a very ambitious and comprehensive fundamental rights policy at the level of the european union. first of all, with the entry into force of the lisbon treaty, the charter of fundamental rights is legally binding, and this legally binding charter is the most modern qualification of fundamental rights in the world in terms of political commitment for fundamental rights, of legibility and of legal certainty, and it entrenches all the rights found in the convention. the meaning and scope of these rights are the same as those laid down by the convention, but the charter goes further. in it we find, for example, the so-called third generation of fundamental rights: data protection, guarantees on bioethics, on good and transparent administration. the level of protection provided by the charter must always be at least as high as that of the convention. in many cases it goes beyond. secondly, there is the promotion of fundamental rights as a priority of the stockholm programme, setting the strategic guidelines for developing an area of freedom, security and justice in europe. thirdly, there is the creation of a new portfolio – justice, fundamental rights and citizenship – which shows how much importance the commission attaches to strengthening the action of the commission in this area. then, fourthly, the accession of the eu to the convention. it will guarantee that any person claiming to be a victim of a violation of the convention by an institution or by a body of the union is able to bring a complaint against the union before the strasbourg court under the same conditions as those applying to complaints brought against member states. in political terms accession means that the european union reaffirms the pivotal role played by the convention’s system for the protection of human rights in europe – in an enlarged europe, not only in the european union – but by acceding to this convention the european union puts its weight behind the strasbourg system, and this is a system of external judicial control in the area of fundamental rights because now we are submitting our legal order fully and formally to that control. this, of course, will enhance the credibility both internally and externally of the eu’s very strong commitment to fundamental rights. by mid-march the commission had proposed a negotiation mandate to the council. protocol 8 of the lisbon treaty requires a certain number of substantive guarantees to be provided for in an agreement relating to accession because we have to preserve the specific characteristics of union law and the commission’s recommendation to the council takes full account of these requirements. i just want to mention two of them. it is clear that the union’s competence and powers, as defined in the treaties, may not be affected by the accession, and the provision in the accession agreement will have to make this very clear. likewise, the accession of the european union may not affect either the situation of individual member states in relation to the european court of human rights or the protocols there or the reservations. the negotiations should therefore ensure that the accession agreement creates obligations under the substantive provisions of the conventions only with regard to acts and measures adopted by the institutions or by the bodies of the union. now the commission is seeking a smooth insertion of the european union into the system of the convention. the accession should therefore preserve the substantive and procedural features of that system. however, the accession must meet two requirements. first, as i said already, the specific characteristics of the law of the european union have to be preserved; safeguarding the court of justice and its prerogatives following accession is an important issue. there are interesting proposals on the table which aim at involving the court of justice in situations where the compatibility of a legal act of the union is at stake before the strasbourg court, without a preliminary reference having been made. these proposals can probably be designed in such a way as not to require a treaty amendment and they deserve careful analysis and discussion in the council working party. i know that the spanish presidency is doing everything in order to bring these discussions forward. second, it is important to deal with the specific situation of the union as a distinct legal entity, vested with autonomous powers, which will become a contracting party side-by-side with the member states to a mechanism which was not, initially, designed for this purpose – but it was designed for the member states – and therefore a limited number of technical and procedural adaptations to the conventions are necessary with regard to the specific nature of union law. among these is the so-called ‘co-respondent mechanism’. it is of particular importance to take account of the decentralised implementation of union law by member states. by that mechanism the union will receive the right to join the proceedings as a co-respondent in cases brought against a member state when union law is at stake. from an institutional point of view i would also like to stress the commission’s position that representatives of the european union should participate in the bodies of the convention on an equal footing with the representatives of other contracting parties. that means, for instance, that a judge elected for each contracting party is one of the founding principles of the convention. this principle ensures that each legal system is represented within the court; it is also a reflection of the collective guarantee system established by the convention in which each contracting party is required to participate, and that means that we need a permanent full judge elected by the union who enjoys the same status and has the same duties as his peers and who intervenes potentially in all cases. an ad hoc judge who intervenes only in cases brought against the union or involving union law would not be sufficient. as for the method of electing this judge, the normal procedure provided for in the convention should also apply here. this means that the parliamentary assembly of the council of europe elects such a judge from a list of three candidates presented by the european union. we believe that an appropriate number of members of the european parliament should be allowed to participate in sessions of the parliamentary assembly when it elects the judges of the strasbourg court. i would like to thank the rapporteurs of the afco and libe committees, mr jáuregui and mrs gál, for their excellent cooperation on the file, and the hearing which was organised by the afco committee on 18 march was really of great use. i am also happy that the spanish presidency of the council gave high priority to this file. i am therefore confident that we will be able to start the negotiations on accession after the summer. i will ensure that the commission, as the union’s negotiator, will keep parliament fully informed throughout the negotiation process. madam president, i do not believe that it is necessary on such a day to underline once more how important fundamental rights are for europe and how important they are for all the acts we are proposing. i am sure the union will not find it difficult to meet the standards of the convention, but adhering to the convention will certainly enhance the protection of fundamental rights in europe, and by this i mean of each and every single human being who lives in europe.

in writing. today we gave the green light to the establishment of the european asylum support office. the benefits are many. the asylum support office will play a key role in the completion of a single european asylum area. it will rapidly set up an operational body to coordinate and enhance cooperation between member states on asylum matters by promoting convergence between different national practices. the service will also contribute to the convergence of eu regulations on the right of asylum. in view of all these benefits, and also of the consensus that has been shown by both the member states and the european institutions on the creation of the european bureau, i was very happy to vote in favour of the proposal to create it.
in writing. achieving the 20-20-20 target by 2020, i.e. a 20% reduction in energy consumption, increasing the share of energy from renewable sources in total energy consumption by 20% and increasing energy efficiency by 20%, requires coordinated and targeted action by both the eu and the member states. in particular, improving the energy performance of buildings is the most effective way to reduce energy consumption and emissions by 20% in sectors outside the ets. in particular, energy-efficient buildings can achieve on average 30% more energy savings than conventional buildings. in addition, energy-efficient buildings use less water and have lower maintenance and utility costs. i therefore voted in favour of the energy performance of buildings directive because it is expected to have a major impact on the lives of european citizens, as it directly affects the buildings in which they live and use. moreover, investments in energy efficiency and renewable energy will create millions of jobs and contribute to the eu's economic growth, while also helping to save much needed financial resources currently spent on the maintenance of energy-intensive buildings.

member of the commission. − the visa policy of the european union is harmonised and it is a common policy. it is based on three legal instruments, applicable to member states, namely regulation (ec) no 539/2001, listing the third countries whose nationals are subject to visa requirements and those who are not; secondly the visa code covering all procedures and conditions for issuing short-stay schengen visas; and finally regulation (ec) no 1683/95 establishing the uniform format for visas. these rules apply to nationals of all third countries subject to visa requirement. the first regulation i referred to establishes a list of third countries whose nationals must be in possession of visas when crossing external borders; this is the so-called ‘negative’ list. there is also the positive list: those nationals who are exempt from that requirement on the basis of different criteria, amongst which reciprocity is a basic principle. this regulation is applicable to all eu member states except for the united kingdom and ireland and also to iceland, norway and switzerland. in accordance with the principle of reciprocity, the eu considers that, in the case of nationals from third country who are exempted from the visa requirement for travelling to the eu member states, the third country should provide reciprocal treatment for the eu citizens by exempting them from the visa requirement when travelling to that country. when a third country on the positive list maintains or introduces a visa obligation for nationals of one, two or more member states, the reciprocity mechanisms apply. this is the framework in which the commission could take steps to obtain the restoration of the visa-free travel by the third country, or if that is not achievable, to propose retaliatory measures on the temporary restoration of the visa requirement for nationals of that third country. this system has proven to be quite efficient, as the steps taken by the commission and drawn up in the periodical reciprocity report show, and under this reciprocity mechanism, applicable since 2005, 75 cases of non-reciprocity concerning 13 third countries of the positive list were notified by member states. since then reciprocity has been established with most of these 13 countries, such as japan, panama, singapore, australia, uruguay and costa rica, and recently the commission concluded negotiations on a visa waiver with brazil, and that will be submitted to you and to the council very soon. problems of non-reciprocity continue to exist for certain member states vis-à-vis the us and canada, and this is something that we always bring up with these countries. the mechanism does not apply in case a third country on the negative list maintains or imposes the visa obligation only on nationals of one or more member countries, or when the third country applies different conditions for citizens of different member states. the community acquis does not contain rules for such cases and does not provide a specific mechanism, so it is very difficult for the eu to intervene.

member of the commission. − madam president, i fully agree that we have to look at this question in a wider context, in this case in the context of the financial and economic crisis. in the last two years we saw that this was a test of competition policies no matter whether it concerned the financial sector, the automotive sector or, in this case, the housing sector, and it was also a test of our social policies, whether it concerned children or the elderly or the homeless. in this set of questions which i received, these two issues – competition and social policies – overlap. that is why it is even more complex than it would be outside the context of the crisis. the crisis demonstrated an enormous market failure, not only in the financial sector but also in the housing sector, and it became very clear that market forces alone cannot resolve these problems, not only for the extremely poor, but also for larger groups of society. that is why i would be strictly against any principle that would restrict the concept of social housing to only the poorest groups in society, especially with respect to the diversity of european countries and the principle of subsidiarity. i would certainly insist on leaving the definitions in this context to the member states themselves as i have said already in my introductory speech. going back to the dutch case, which has been the focus of the discussion, i would like to repeat that the commission is not imposing the criteria that have been set in the dutch context to any other country. in full respect of subsidiarity, it is for the member states to decide the actual conditionality of social housing. this is confirmed by the decision concerning the dutch state aid scheme, and i would like to recall that the limits set by the dutch authorities – which apply only in the netherlands – cover 43% of the dutch population, which is certainly well beyond the poorest groups. the dutch decision, moreover, has confirmed that the social mix and social cohesion are valid public policy objectives for which state aid may be justified, and not only for those living in extreme poverty or at risk of poverty. i think the social distress in this over the last few years has destabilised society on a much wider scale, and that is why we have to be sensitive to this. i would also need to add that the commission only verifies aid given to housing companies. any subsidy given directly to citizens is not subject to state aid rules. the discussion also touched upon a wider context, which is social services of general interest. that is why i need to address this as well and emphasise that beyond housing, other services of general interest and in particular other social services play a preventive and socially cohesive role which is targeted at the whole population independently of wealth or income. the commission made this point clear in its 2007 communication when it highlighted the objectives and principles of organisation of social services. the commission is committed to promoting the quality of social services. for instance we support the development of a quality framework for social services of general interest within the social protection committee. a few final thoughts in closing my answer. since some of the questions concerned a longer timescale, spanning into the next financial perspective, i extremely vulnerable marginalised groups in a variety of member states. this also highlights the importance of having a very diversified view because countries are different in terms of their social needs, and certain decisions and solutions that are applied in high-income countries certainly do not necessarily have to be followed – and definitely not imposed – in other member states.

the next item is the commission statement on safety and prevention measures on the european union's offshore oil platforms.
the s&d group is calling for a new approach to the problem of the environment. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. the recent explosion in the gulf of mexico occurred on a platform that was only built in 2001, and its subsequent sinking is causing one of the greatest ecological disasters to date. so far, 29 days after the accident, it has not been possible to stop the leak and, as mr sonik said, over 5,000 tonnes of oil are being spilled into the sea every day in this bay. this huge pollution is occurring at a time when ovulation peaks for many species, many of which are endangered. these are five of the seven species of sea turtles, dolphins, a great many whales and a great many important marine mammals. fate, and man suffers! this explosion, this accident, happened in an area that is just beginning to recover from the wounds left by hurricane katrina, and the explosion itself caused the death of 11 people. but in america they take action. congress in 1981 voted a moratorium that imposed a ban on offshore oil drilling in 85 percent of america's coastal waters. the obama administration has confirmed the moratorium after the crash, despite initial statements to the contrary. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's fishing fleet is not disrupted by the oil spills. there are hundreds of offshore platforms currently in operation, both for oil and for natural gas. the recent accident in the gulf of mexico really confirmed the risk of literal disaster to the marine environment from offshore oil rigs. however, european legislation excludes the exploration and exploitation of offshore oil resources from the scope of the seveso directive on the management of major-accident hazards involving dangerous substances. the recent disaster shows us that no one can guarantee that a similar disaster could not happen in the european union and that sometimes simply increasing preventive measures is not enough. the obama administration, faced with the scale of the disaster, has folded. is it not time, in addition to additional preventive measures, for the european union to introduce a european moratorium, which will henceforth prohibit offshore oil drilling in european union waters, in line with the us? we must act immediately, before a predicted gulf of mexico crime actually knocks on our door.

the gulf of mexico, man is basically far from the source of danger, far from technical safety. i also trust our member states. we have every reason to trust our national authorities and our technical level of cooperative security between the european union and our member states, which are neighbouring countries. we have of course also had to consider the question of safety in the case of nord stream. there were complex safety and permitting procedures, all of which were carried out, and i would like to say that nord stream will probably be the most advanced and secure gas pipeline in the world. there are also crucial differences. if there's ever a problem in the gas pipeline, you can stop the gas at the source or at the coast. nord stream is not comparable to what is happening in the gulf of mexico. ultimately, we have to find a way out of oil, but that will take decades. every one of us in politics and society must go to him. and on the way there and in the meantime, we have to
